title: system_server Boot and System Service Architecture

scout.purpose: Understand system_server boot and system service architecture as a causal Android engineering system rather than a vocabulary item.
scout.realWorldUse: Expert Android diagnosis requires tracing responsibility through processes, framework services, threads, queues, graphics buffers, and system composition.
scout.outcome: You can explain, inspect, test, and safely apply system_server boot and system service architecture.

blocks.text: Zygote also forks system_server, a privileged process that creates the main framework service environment. SystemServer progresses through bootstrap, core, and other service startup phases, publishes Binder endpoints, advances boot phases, and coordinates dependencies. Services such as ActivityManager, ActivityTaskManager, PackageManager, and parts of WindowManager expose framework behavior, while many native daemons and HAL services remain in separate processes. system_server is central but is not the entire operating system.

blocks.text: A framework manager obtained from Context is usually a client facade that calls a remote Binder service; its Java object in the app does not own global truth. Service startup order and boot phases prevent consumers using dependencies before ready. Watchdogs, permissions, SELinux, Binder identity, and isolated native services reduce damage but system_server failure is device-critical. Slow synchronous calls into it can block app main threads, and app Binder callbacks can in turn block service pools, creating cross-process latency chains.

blocks.text: Use service list, dumpsys, cmd, Perfetto Binder slices, and AOSP SystemServer source to map ownership without changing production state. For a public API call, identify app facade, AIDL interface, service implementation, persisted authority, native or HAL hop, and callback. Treat internal class names and boot ordering as release-dependent implementation details. Platform changes require compatibility, permissions, tests, watchdog awareness, and boot evidence; app developers should use public APIs rather than reflection into hidden services.

Platform internals are a causal map for diagnosis, not an invitation to depend on hidden APIs. Trace ownership across process, thread, Binder, token, queue, buffer, and display boundaries; distinguish public contracts from release-specific implementation. Use AOSP source matching the device branch, Perfetto, dumpsys, logcat, bug reports, and controlled experiments as complementary evidence. Record Android build, device, configuration, process state, workload, and timestamps. Test death, cancellation, reentrancy, backpressure, configuration, multi-window, and resource pressure. When a private class or trace label changes, the explanation should still stand at the responsibility level. Production apps use supported APIs, while platform changes require compatibility tests, security policy, boot and performance evidence, and safe rollback.

blocks.title: Common systems trap
blocks.text: Watch carefully for this common failure mode in production: Calling getSystemService returns a local manager object, but assuming all work is local hides Binder latency, remote failure, permission checks, and system ownership.

trap_check.mistake: Calling getSystemService returns a local manager object, but assuming all work is local hides Binder latency, remote failure, permission checks, and system ownership.
trap_check.why: It collapses distinct ownership or timing boundaries and can produce a confident but incorrect diagnosis.
trap_check.fix: Trace the complete causal path with matching source and runtime evidence before changing the system.

trap_check.mistake: Depending on a hidden API, internal class name, trace label, or one device observation as a stable application contract.
trap_check.why: Platform implementation and vendor behavior can change while public compatibility guarantees remain different.
trap_check.fix: Use internals for explanation and diagnosis, but implement app behavior through supported APIs and test across versions.

recall.prompt: What does a framework manager object usually represent?
recall.answer: A local client facade or proxy for state and operations owned by a framework service, often across Binder.

recall.prompt: What must be recorded with systems evidence?
recall.answer: The Android and app build, device, configuration, starting state, workload, process or thread context, and exact capture method.

recall.prompt: How should application code use platform-internals knowledge?
recall.answer: Use it to diagnose and reason about public behavior, not to depend on hidden implementation APIs or names.
